source.citation: Written for Blackout, 2026-10-09, from the ABFM 2025 In-Training Examination critiques, items 51 to 63. Each question cites its item. Authoring batch for the ITE pool; review before trusting.

questions.q: A small cardioembolic stroke with new atrial fibrillation. When is anticoagulation started?
questions.why: Without an antiplatelet alongside. A 2024 trial found starting within four days safe, and the small infarcts go first; large ones with a risk of haemorrhagic conversion wait towards the end of the window.

questions.q: What makes atrial fibrillation nonvalvular for the purpose of choosing an anticoagulant?
questions.a: No significant mitral stenosis or mechanical valve
d: No mitral regurgitation of any grade on echo
No prior valve surgery or repair of any kind
A normal echocardiogram in every respect
questions.why: Mild mitral regurgitation does not count. Nonvalvular fibrillation gets a direct oral anticoagulant in preference to warfarin.

questions.q: After a cardioembolic stroke, which patient waits the full 14 days before anticoagulation?
questions.a: One with a large infarct at risk of bleeding
d: One started on a direct oral anticoagulant
One with mitral regurgitation on echo
One whose weakness has fully resolved
questions.why: Haemorrhagic conversion is the danger being traded against recurrence. A small infarct with resolving symptoms can start within days.

questions.q: Four days after a STEMI: hypotension, a new systolic murmur, crackles, flat neck veins. What has happened?
questions.why: Acute mitral regurgitation with flash pulmonary oedema and shock. Mechanical complications are rarer than they were, but their in-hospital mortality stays high.

questions.q: How long after a transmural infarction does papillary muscle rupture typically occur?
questions.why: After an infarct in right coronary or circumflex territory, depending on the anatomy. Free wall rupture, which causes tamponade, is rarer still.

questions.q: Which findings point to tamponade rather than papillary muscle rupture after an infarction?
questions.why: Both cause hypotension and tachycardia. The lungs fill with acute mitral regurgitation; the neck veins fill with tamponade.

questions.q: What is the rule for formoterol as an as-needed asthma reliever?
d: Alone as a reliever, like albuterol
questions.why: Its long action is what makes the combination work as a reliever, and its long action unprotected by a steroid is what makes it unsafe alone.

questions.q: By about how much does as-needed ICS-formoterol cut severe exacerbations versus as-needed albuterol?
questions.why: And it beats every regimen that keeps a short-acting reliever, including a daily low-dose steroid with albuterol on top.

questions.q: An intensely itchy, serpiginous red rash on the feet after a trip to Vietnam. What is it?
questions.why: Scabies runs along skin folds in lines of small bumps. Leishmaniasis gives painless ulcers with raised borders. Herpes B gives vesicles at the bite site with flu-like illness.

questions.q: How is cutaneous larva migrans diagnosed and treated?
questions.why: There is no diagnostic test. Incubation is usually 1 to 5 days but can run to a month, and the infection is self-limited.

questions.q: A child treated for Cryptosporidium is well again. When can he swim?
questions.why: Oocysts keep shedding after recovery and survive up to ten days in treated water, which is how one child clears a pool.

questions.q: What is the treatment for Cryptosporidium diarrhoea?
questions.why: Diagnosis is on a stool sample. Severe or prolonged disease earns the antiparasitic; ordinary cases get supportive care.

questions.q: At 36 weeks: headache, right upper quadrant pain, BP 150/95, platelets 43,000, AST 112, proteinuria. What is done?
questions.why: HELLP syndrome. The liver failure belongs to the pregnancy, not the acetaminophen she took, and steroids raise the platelets without touching the liver.

questions.q: From what gestation is HELLP syndrome managed by prompt delivery?
questions.why: Maternal morbidity and mortality run at 10% to 15%, and the deaths come from delay.

questions.q: Which complications drive the maternal mortality of HELLP syndrome?
questions.why: Cardiopulmonary arrest and sepsis complete the list. Each is a reason the evaluation is quick and targeted rather than exhaustive.

questions.q: A first eGFR of 49. Besides a repeat under 60 at three months, what establishes chronic kidney disease?
d: A creatinine rise during a hospital stay
questions.why: Three months is what separates chronic disease from an acute injury, and it can be found in the past as easily as waited for.

questions.q: Fever for six days, red lips, conjunctivitis, rash and a 2-cm neck node at age 4. The serious complication?
questions.why: Kawasaki disease. Echocardiography is done as soon as possible. Anaemia, raised liver enzymes, pyuria and pulmonary oedema occur but are the lesser complications.

questions.q: Untreated, what proportion of children with Kawasaki disease develop cardiovascular abnormalities?
questions.why: Coronary and aortic root dilation, aneurysm, tachycardia, hypotension and shock. Treatment is what brings the figure down.

questions.q: With five days of fever, which features count towards classic Kawasaki disease?
a: Changes of the oral mucous membranes
Oedema of the hands and feet
A cervical node of 1.5 cm or more
questions.why: Four of the five, and the node is unilateral. It is a disease of children under five.

questions.q: A 40-year-old with no breast or ovarian cancer in the family, anxious after a friend tested BRCA2 positive. Advice?
questions.why: The task force recommends against routine assessment, counselling or testing. Colorectal, thyroid and endometrial cancers in relatives do not change that.

questions.q: Which histories call for a formal BRCA risk assessment tool?
a: Breast cancer in a first-degree relative
Tubal or peritoneal cancer in the family
A personal history of breast cancer
d: A close friend with a BRCA mutation
questions.why: Ancestry linked to the mutations also qualifies. Testing comes only after a positive tool and genetic counselling, in that order.

questions.q: A family history of neural tube defects, on 4 mg of folic acid, now at 12 weeks. What is the dose from here?
questions.why: The high dose runs until 12 weeks after conception. Supplementation is on top of dietary folate, not instead of it.

questions.q: Why is high-dose folic acid reduced after the first trimester?
d: Folate is no longer absorbed well
It would mask a B12 deficiency
It raises the chance of twins
questions.why: With a theoretical concern about fetal toxicity from the high dose once the neural tube has closed.

questions.q: When should folic acid supplementation begin for a planned pregnancy?
questions.why: The neural tube closes in the first weeks, often before the pregnancy is known. High-risk pregnancies get the 4 mg dose over that period.

questions.q: Recurrent gout with stage 3 kidney disease and a urate of 8.6. What is started for prevention?
questions.why: Allopurinol stays first-line in kidney disease. The anti-inflammatory cover prevents the flare that starting urate-lowering therapy provokes. Febuxostat is for chronic gout but not first.

questions.q: To what serum urate is allopurinol titrated?
questions.why: Pegloticase is strongly recommended against as a first-line drug, for cost, uncertain safety, and the existence of better options.

questions.q: Which drugs treat an acute gout flare?
questions.why: Urate-lowering drugs prevent the next flare rather than treating this one, and starting one without cover tends to set a flare off.

questions.q: New angina in a patient with aortic stenosis. Besides referral for the valve, what is evaluated?
questions.why: Symptoms turn the prognosis: under half survive two years without replacement, and replacement restores survival to that of age-matched adults. A louder murmur or calcification on echo is not an indication on its own.

questions.q: A few days of sneezing, congestion and watery discharge each spring. What is first-line?
d: A short course of oral steroid
questions.why: Even for mild allergic rhinitis. Antihistamines by either route are less effective, cromolyn needs several doses a day, and there is no infection to treat.

questions.q: What is the place of nasal saline irrigation in allergic rhinitis?
d: A replacement for the steroid spray
questions.why: It rinses allergen from the nose and sits alongside drug treatment, never instead of it.
